newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russia stock market widens investment horizon.
newsitem.headline: New Russia stock market widens investment horizon.

text.p: A new second-tier Russian stock market, which almost doubles the number of quoted companies in what may be the world's hottest market, is gaining respect despite the troubles of working with little-known stocks.

The Russian Trading System's RTS-2 market lists 72 shares, including preferred stock, in a new market of 47 regional companies that traders expect hungry investors to look to more and more as prices of the main RTS system's 89 stocks appreciate.

The RTS 24-share index of leading stocks has gained about 50 percent since the beginning of the year and traders say investors who have chiefly pushed up prices of a dozen or so leading shares are now looking toward less well-known issues.

Regional telecommunication companies, one of the hot potential sectors for 1997, are already leading trade volume on the young RTS-2 system, traders say, adding that the second-tier system has the same essential characteristics as its bigger brother.
"We conduct ourselves just like RTS-1," said trader Andrei Galperin of Creditanstalt-Grant in Moscow.
"I make the same money on them as I make on the main system," said UCB trader Yuri Sychev.
Traders have rushed onto the RTS-2 system since it came on line on Dec. 23.

"The success has been better than we expected," said Alexei Telyatnikov, technical director of the PAUFOR brokers association that manages the computer network linking traders throughout Moscow and Russia.
He said PAUFOR had already received 150 orders for RTS-2 terminals. After about two years of the Russian Trading System, there are 373 RTS terminals, which can be used to trade both sets of shares.

RTS-2 volume has fluctuated between a few hundred thousand dollars to $5 million per day, traders say. The main RTS system saw about $20 million average daily volume before the new year. Since then it has risen sharply to near $80 million on one day.

The national brokers' association NAUFOR is considering promoting several active telecommunications and utilities stocks, and shares in Russia's biggest bank Sberbank, from RTS-2 to the main system, while downgrading 18 illiquid stocks to RTS-2.
Traders say the new market will stimulate liquidity among shares of companies in the far corners of Russia by establishing prices that have not been previously quoted.
"Nobody had seen this market before," said Alfa Capital trader Dmitry Lobanov. "Now we are at least able to figure out price levels."

Using the new system as a training ground of sorts, PAUFOR says it intends to transfer some of the more liquid stocks on to the RTS system in February. Some traders say that as many as half the RTS-2 shares could eventually make the move.

But the system is still dogged by problems of transparency, and PAUFOR has not yet instituted reporting mechanisms akin to those on the main RTS system. PAUFOR currently publishes the results of RTS-2 trading only once a week.

Lobanov said that sourcing shares to buy and sell could be difficult, especially for larger orders, and said spreads on RTS-2 could be as high as 70 percent, since the rules of the system do not require a spread of 10 percent or less, as on RTS.
Low trading minimums -- about $900 on RTS-2 vs. $5,000 on the RTS -- make trade easier, but there is still a scarcity of stock.
"If anyone has some paper, he can put out his offer and make a monopoly market," one trader said.
Traders and brokerages themselves do not know the value, or the business, of many of the newly-listed companies.
"Maybe three of the 10 market makers can tell you what some of these companies are," said one trader.
Company managers in regions relatively untouched by reform have to learn how to serve investors, operators say.
